query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, toughness retention at elevated temperatures is governed by the morphology of the grain boundaries. Specifically, inducing serration in the grain boundaries (via controlled cooling during post-solution heat treatment) can reduce local strain concentration and delay intergranular crack initiation, thereby maintaining ductility and extending creep rupture life.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy fabricated by selective laser melting (SLM) exhibiting straight, nearly planar grain boundaries and subject to a known hot ductility drop at elevated temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply a slower cooling rate during the solution heat treatment to promote the coarsening of precipitates that induce a serrated grain boundary morphology.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under high-temperature conditions (e.g., around 650°C) including tensile and creep tests, comparing alloys with conventional straight versus induced serrated grain boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary morphology, specifically the transformation from straight to serrated grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The serrated morphology distributes local strains more evenly along the boundaries, reduces stress localization, and offers resistance against intergranular cracking. This modification mitigates the formation of weak sites that typically lead to brittle failure at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy with serrated grain boundaries will exhibit a significant increase in tensile ductility (e.g., an improvement factor similar to previously observed ~3.5× increase) and substantially enhanced creep rupture life (potentially in the order of hundreds fold more life) when compared to the baseline alloy with straight boundaries.
generation.baseline: The unmodified high-entropy alloy processed by SLM with straight grain boundaries and exhibiting a notable hot ductility drop (e.g., reduction in elongation and creep life) under similar conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for high-entropy alloys processed by SLM and heat-treated in similar regimes (e.g., near 650°C testing conditions) where grain boundary controlled mechanisms are dominant. Its applicability to alloys processed by other methods or under significantly different temperatures remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how variations in alloy composition, precipitate chemistry, or alternative processing routes might modify the degree to which grain boundary serration can control toughness. The precise quantitative improvement in mechanical properties may vary depending on these factors.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples using SLM. Subject one set to a standard solution heat treatment resulting in straight grain boundaries (baseline) and the other set to a modified slower cooling heat treatment designed to induce serrated grain boundaries. Perform tensile and creep tests at 650°C on both groups.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with induced serrated grain boundaries do not show a statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility and creep rupture life compared to the baseline samples with straight grain boundaries, or if strain localization patterns do not differ markedly between the two groups, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
